final_proposal.title: The Extra Inch
final_proposal.idea: Inside every well-made Dior couture garment, a hidden inch of seam allowance lets the piece be taken in, let out and refitted for decades. The campaign reveals that inch as the house's quiet promise of a long life. Films open garments to show the secret, and real owners return for their next fitting as bodies, lives and occasions change. Atelier hands, credited by first name, perform each refit. A published Inch Standard backs the claim, and a refit service makes it usable. Resoling, re-edging and re-strapping extend it to accessories as 'the next inch'. Later, re-gifting opens the story to a second owner. Luxury becomes a long relationship with a garment, not a purchase.
follow_up_questions: What other hidden details of craftsmanship in your own brand could stand as a quiet promise, and how would you make them visible without turning them into a lecture?
What commitment or standard could you publish so that a longevity claim is something customers can hold you to rather than just a message?
How could a product or service be designed to change with its owner over time, and which life moments would make the best stories?

element_review.selected_core_idea: Dior reveals the hidden extra inch of seam allowance inside its well-made garments as a quiet, ownable promise of a long life, and frames refitting, repair and passing on as the 'next inch' of a garment's story.

candidate_elements.element: Real owners' emotional stories, with clients returning to see their pieces refitted or reborn
candidate_elements.purpose: Adds emotional warmth to a technical product truth and offsets the risk that the seam-allowance detail feels dry.
candidate_elements.reason: The main concern with C2 is dryness. Real refit stories (a wedding dress let out for a daughter, a jacket taken in after decades) make the inch human. Real clients in the work also keep the claim honest. The staged damage spectacle and the romanticising of flaws are left out.

candidate_elements.element: Staged couture show built on moth holes, tears and flaws reinterpreted as design signatures
candidate_elements.purpose: Would give the campaign a provocative, press-worthy spectacle.
candidate_elements.reason: It risks romanticising damage and devaluing expensive pieces. It is also a one-off, and it pulls the idea toward celebrating wear rather than a promise of longevity and care.

candidate_elements.element: Atelier hands performing the refits, shown in close-up and credited by first name
candidate_elements.purpose: Shows who delivers the promise, makes the service tangible and gives the idea a human face.
candidate_elements.reason: It makes the inch credible, because viewers see it being let out or taken in. It also supports the atelier talent story. It is used as a storytelling layer inside C2, not as a standalone craft-hero campaign, so it avoids the forgettable trope.

candidate_elements.element: House-certified pre-owned programme with numbered labels recording previous wearers
candidate_elements.purpose: Gives a concrete reuse offer for later owners and lets Dior control the secondhand experience.
candidate_elements.reason: It is a business-model decision needing heavy internal alignment, with risks of cannibalisation and privacy issues. It stays as a possible later extension. The proposal keeps only a light 'passing on' offer (a refit before re-gifting).

candidate_elements.element: A published Dior construction standard: a defined seam allowance and repair-readiness criteria for eligible pieces
candidate_elements.purpose: Backs the longevity promise with verifiable commitments and reduces greenwashing exposure.
candidate_elements.reason: The main risk of C2 is an unbacked 'built to last' claim. A public standard, plus clear statements of which pieces qualify, makes the promise accountable and ownable.

candidate_elements.element: 'Next inch' equivalents for leather goods, shoes and accessories: resoling, re-edging, re-strapping, re-stitching
candidate_elements.purpose: Extends the metaphor across categories where seam allowances do not apply.
candidate_elements.reason: Without it the idea covers only couture and ready-to-wear. The 'next inch' as a unit of renewal lets the whole house take part without stretching the literal seam story.

candidate_elements.element: An 'Inch Service' for booking refits, alterations and re-gifting preparation, including an inch-marked label or tape inside eligible garments
candidate_elements.purpose: Turns the message into behaviour and gives clients something to do.
candidate_elements.reason: It converts the idea from storytelling into a service with a visible symbol. It also supports the claim that the garment is designed to change, as long as atelier capacity is planned.

revisions_after_selection.reason: The technical seam-allowance detail risks feeling dry. Human stories of garments changing across life moments make it emotional and shareable.

revisions_after_selection.change: Added atelier hands as the people who perform and are credited for each refit, used inside the story rather than as a separate campaign.
revisions_after_selection.reason: It makes the promise tangible and credible without falling into the generic craft-hero trope.

revisions_after_selection.change: Added a published Dior construction and repair standard that sets out which pieces carry the extra inch and what the house commits to.
revisions_after_selection.reason: It answers the greenwashing risk by making the longevity claim specific, verifiable and accountable.

revisions_after_selection.change: Defined 'the next inch' as a wider renewal principle covering resoling, re-edging and re-strapping for leather goods, shoes and accessories.
revisions_after_selection.reason: It solves the limit of the seam metaphor outside garments, so the campaign covers the whole house.

final_proposal.title: The Extra Inch
final_proposal.idea: Inside every well-made Dior couture garment, a hidden inch of seam allowance lets the piece be taken in, let out and refitted over decades. The Extra Inch makes that secret visible: a quiet promise that a Dior piece is designed to change with its owner. Films follow real clients and the atelier hands who refit their pieces, from a gown let out for a daughter to a jacket taken in after thirty years. A published construction standard backs the claim. An Inch Service lets clients book refits and prepare pieces for re-gifting, while resoling, re-edging and re-strapping extend 'the next inch' to shoes and leather goods. Luxury becomes a long relationship with a garment, not a single purchase.

required_elements.what_it_does: Makes the idea instantly recognisable and extendable across film, retail, product and service.

revisions_after_selection.reason: Seam allowances don't apply to non-sewn categories, so the metaphor needed a clear extension to avoid looking couture-only.

final_proposal.title: The Extra Inch
final_proposal.idea: Inside every well-made Dior piece is a secret: a hidden inch of fabric, left so the garment can change with its owner. The Extra Inch makes that inch Dior's promise of a long life. It becomes a published construction standard for new collections, a visible marker sewn inside the lining, and a refit and repair service where atelier hands take in, let out, re-hem and revive. Leather, shoes and accessories get their own next inch: re-edging, resoling, re-strapping. Real owners tell the stories, from a dress refitted for a daughter's wedding to a coat passed to a friend. Luxury stops being a purchase and becomes a relationship: every refit is simply the next inch of the story.
follow_up_questions: What should Dior be willing to commit to publicly (minimum allowances, repair guarantees, turnaround times) so that the inch is a promise people can hold the house to?

What moment of passing on (a wedding, a birthday, a first job, a hand-me-down between friends) is most worth owning, and how could the house mark it without turning it into a resale transaction?

final_proposal.title: The Extra Inch
final_proposal.idea: Inside a well-made Dior garment, extra fabric is folded into the seams. This hidden inch, called a seam allowance, lets the atelier take the piece in, let it out or refit it for decades. The Extra Inch makes that detail Dior's quiet promise of a long life. Dior publishes a minimum standard for it, then opens refit appointments, so owners can adjust, repair or pass on a piece. For shoes and bags, the next inch means resoling, re-edging or re-strapping. Real owners and atelier hands tell the stories. The inch becomes a motif, a unit of measure and a service name. Luxury becomes a long relationship with a garment, not a single purchase.
follow_up_questions: What would Dior have to build or promise, such as a lifetime refit entitlement or a published standard, for owners to believe the hidden inch is real?
Which moments in a garment's life, such as a change of body, a gift or a handover to a daughter, are most emotionally powerful as 'the next inch'?
How could the inch be made visible without spoiling the garment, such as a coloured thread, a measured label or a tailor's chalk mark?
